---
title: "Marriage and generation in the United States"
execute:
  echo: false
---

## What share of adults are married?

This page uses the U.S. Census Bureau's 2023 American Community Survey (ACS)
Public Use Microdata Sample (PUMS) to compare marital status across generations.
The Census does not ask people which generation they belong to, so generation is
estimated from age using Pew Research Center birth-year ranges. The estimates
below represent adults ages 18 and older.

To run this analysis, request a free [Census API key](https://api.census.gov/data/key_signup.html)
and add it to your local R environment with
`tidycensus::census_api_key("YOUR KEY", install = TRUE)`. Do not put your key in
this project. Restart R before rendering the page.

```{r}
#| label: setup
#| message: false

library(tidyverse)
library(tidycensus)
```

```{r}
#| label: load-census-data
#| cache: true

us_adults <- get_pums(
  variables = c("AGEP", "MAR", "PWGTP"),
  state = "all",
  year = 2023,
  survey = "acs1",
  variables_filter = list(AGEP = 18:99)
)
```

`PWGTP` is the ACS person weight, used here to estimate the U.S. population
represented by the sample. The cohort age ranges below use 2023 minus the
published birth-year boundaries; age at interview can place a small number of
people near a generation boundary in an adjacent cohort.

```{r}
#| label: summarize-by-generation

generation_levels <- c(
  "Gen Z", "Millennials", "Gen X", "Baby Boomers",
  "Silent Generation", "Greatest Generation"
)

marital_status_labels <- c(
  "1" = "Married",
  "2" = "Widowed",
  "3" = "Divorced",
  "4" = "Separated",
  "5" = "Never married"
)

marital_status_by_generation <- us_adults |>
  mutate(
    generation = case_when(
      AGEP <= 26 ~ "Gen Z",
      AGEP <= 42 ~ "Millennials",
      AGEP <= 58 ~ "Gen X",
      AGEP <= 77 ~ "Baby Boomers",
      AGEP <= 95 ~ "Silent Generation",
      TRUE ~ "Greatest Generation"
    ),
    generation = factor(generation, levels = generation_levels),
    marital_status = recode(as.character(MAR), !!!marital_status_labels)
  ) |>
  filter(!is.na(marital_status)) |>
  group_by(generation, marital_status) |>
  summarise(weighted_people = sum(PWGTP), .groups = "drop") |>
  group_by(generation) |>
  mutate(percent = 100 * weighted_people / sum(weighted_people)) |>
  ungroup()

married_by_generation <- marital_status_by_generation |>
  filter(marital_status == "Married")
```

```{r}
#| label: plot-marriage-by-generation
#| fig-cap: "Estimated share of U.S. adults who were married in 2023, by generation."

ggplot(married_by_generation, aes(x = generation, y = percent)) +
  geom_col(fill = "#3973ac") +
  geom_text(
    aes(label = scales::percent(percent / 100, accuracy = 1)),
    vjust = -0.4
  ) +
  scale_y_continuous(
    labels = scales::label_percent(scale = 1),
    limits = c(0, 100),
    expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.08))
  ) +
  labs(
    x = NULL,
    y = "Adults currently married",
    caption = "Source: U.S. Census Bureau, 2023 ACS 1-year PUMS; weighted with PWGTP."
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 25, hjust = 1))
```

The table gives the estimated marital-status distribution for each generation.
In the ACS, "married" is a marital-status response; "separated" is reported
separately.

```{r}
#| label: marital-status-table

marital_status_by_generation |>
  select(generation, marital_status, percent) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = marital_status, values_from = percent) |>
  select(generation, Married, Widowed, Divorced, Separated, `Never married`) |>
  arrange(generation) |>
  mutate(across(where(is.numeric), \(x) round(x, 1))) |>
  knitr::kable(
    col.names = c("Generation", "Married (%)", "Widowed (%)", "Divorced (%)",
                  "Separated (%)", "Never married (%)"),
    caption = "Estimated marital status of U.S. adults by generation, 2023."
  )
```

## Data and definitions

- **Census source:** [2023 ACS 1-year PUMS](https://www.census.gov/programs-surveys/acs/microdata.html).
  PUMS contains anonymized person-level survey records; the person weight
  (`PWGTP`) lets the sample estimate population totals and percentages.
- **Generation boundaries:** Pew Research Center's [generation definitions](https://www.pewresearch.org/short-reads/2019/01/17/where-millennials-end-and-generation-z-begins/):
  Gen Z begins in 1997; Millennials are 1981-1996; Gen X is 1965-1980;
  Baby Boomers are 1946-1964; the Silent Generation is 1928-1945; and the
  Greatest Generation was born before 1928.
- **Coverage:** Only adults are included. Thus, the Gen Z estimate covers only
  adults in that generation. Generation is not a Census variable; boundaries
  and age-at-interview mean these groupings are approximate. These are weighted
  point estimates and do not show sampling margins of error.
